title: Early Voting Kicks Off as Midterms Could Flip Congress
summary:
HENRICO, Va. — In-person voting for this year's midterm elections began Friday, launching the final six weeks before Americans decide which party should lead Congress through a cost-of-living crisis, a prolonged war in Iran and other pressing issues.

At a voting location in Fairfax, Virginia, 18-year-old college student Sanya Singhal arrived well before the site opened to be among the first. "Why not just have a little fun in life, you know, try to be the first early voter?" she said. "I really want to participate in my democracy." At a suburban Richmond polling place, a worker rang a bell as the building opened and about a dozen voters filed in.

The Nov. 3 election will determine whether Republicans maintain control of the U.S. House and Senate. If Democrats retake Congress, it would alter the trajectory of the final two years of President Donald Trump's term, most likely leading to investigations and other oversight efforts.

Voters are weighing deep anxieties: rising gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, the looming risks of artificial intelligence and Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement. William Curry, a 74-year-old retiree who calls himself a libertarian-leaning independent conservative, voted for Republicans but criticized the Iran conflict. "He's in a mess he can't get rid of," Curry said of Trump. In Sioux Falls, South Dakota, 67-year-old Bill Goehring voted for a mix of Democrats and independents, saying Trump's "dictatorial tendencies are bad for America."

Election administrators say they are prepared and confident the vote will be secure. Still, Trump has continued efforts to reshape how elections are run, through court challenges, a federal hunt for noncitizen voters and pressure on officials to share sensitive voter data. This week, the Supreme Court rejected his bid to restrict mail ballots. Virginia's attorney general said Thursday that the administration may have violated state law after a whistleblower accused federal employees of misrepresenting themselves on voter lookup tools. Research continues to show noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research said he expects Trump to continue "his disinformation campaign," but added, "ultimately the process will hold as it has in past years."
why_it_matters: Elections like this decide who writes laws on prices, technology, and foreign wars that today's teenagers will live with for decades, and they test whether people still trust the systems that count their votes.

background_read: Midterm elections are held every two years, halfway through a president's four-year term, and they decide all 435 seats in the House of Representatives plus roughly a third of the 100-member Senate. Because the president's party has historically tended to lose seats in midterms, these elections often act as a check on the White House.

Early in-person voting has expanded across U.S. states over the past two decades, letting voters cast a ballot before Election Day. Election rules are mostly written and run by the states rather than the federal government, which is why court challenges and federal pressure over mail ballots and voter data are so fiercely contested.

The Supreme Court (the highest U.S. court, with nine justices) rejected the president's attempt to restrict mail ballots this week. David Becker works at the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that studies how elections are actually administered, and researchers across the political spectrum have repeatedly found that noncitizen voting is extremely rare.

The article also mentions a prolonged war in Iran; Iran is a country in the Middle East whose relationship with the United States has been tense for decades. President Donald Trump has been in office since 2025 and has pushed to change how elections are run through lawsuits and pressure on officials.

perspectives.description: The opening of early voting shows the machinery of democracy working: young first-time voters like Sanya Singhal line up voluntarily, and administrators report they are prepared. High turnout would give the result stronger legitimacy, whichever party wins.

President Trump's lawsuits, the federal search for noncitizen voters, and demands for sensitive voter data have convinced many supporters that elections are insecure, even though research repeatedly shows noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. Critics warn that this erodes confidence in results before a single ballot is counted.

Midterms have traditionally punished the sitting president's party, making them a referendum on the economy and foreign policy rather than on a single leader. With gas and grocery prices rising and a war in Iran dragging on, this election fits that pattern, even as the fight over election rules themselves becomes a major issue.

If Democrats take Congress, expect subpoenas, hearings, and blocked legislation; if Republicans hold on, the White House gains room to push its agenda further. Either way, the legal battles over mail ballots and voter data are likely to continue into the next presidential cycle.
